extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and practitioners assessing novelty/disclosure under French law and the European Patent Convention (EPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when information (including new-media/internet disclosures) constitutes prior art affecting novelty and inventive step under French law and the European Patent Convention, and for evidentiary proof of such disclosures. Covers means, timing, place, beneficiaries, confidentiality exceptions, grace periods, and standards of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute and objective novelty (Finnish formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Finnish patent system is based on absolute and objective novelty: patents may be granted only for inventions which are new in relation to what was known before the filing date of the patent application and which also differ essentially therefrom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time of disclosure, place or media of disclosure are irrelevant; all information available to the public by any means anywhere in the world prior to the filing date is relevant. Attention should be paid to potential abuse enabled by new technologies; consider third-party services for timestamping/verifying Internet disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art identical to the invention destroys novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is considered new only if it is not comprised in the state of the art; an antériorité identical to the invention destroys novelty (art. L.611-11 CPI / Art. 54 EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty look for identity with the claimed subject-matter; any disclosed information that is the same as the invention negates novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (non-obviousness) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, for a person skilled in the art, it does not follow in an obvious manner from the state of the art (art. L.611-14 CPI / Art. 56 EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior disclosure can destroy inventive step if the invention would be obvious to the skilled person in view of that prior art, possibly in combination with other state-of-the-art elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requires both novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention lacking novelty or inventive step is not patentable (art. L.611-10 CPI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both criteria must be satisfied; lack of either suffices to refuse or invalidate a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of pending unpublished applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished pending applications are taken into account for assessment of novelty but not for assessment of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French and European pending, non-published applications affect novelty only; treat them differently in inventive-step analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ‘state of the art’ / what constitutes disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art is constituted by everything made accessible to the public before the filing date by a written or oral description, by use, or by any other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be a disclosure, technical information must have been made accessible to the public by any medium; the statutory language is broad ('tout autre moyen').

rubrics_metrics.name: No exclusion of means of disclosure (everything can disclose)
rubrics_metrics.description: French law and the Munich Convention do not exclude any means of disclosure; oral disclosures, uses, electronic disclosures, etc., all can qualify as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different means of disclosure may raise specific evidentiary problems, but once established the legal effect is the same regardless of medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and place of disclosure irrelevant (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French law and the Munich Convention make no distinction between recent and ancient disclosures or as to the place of disclosure; any antériorité divulguée is part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While date/place do not affect whether something is prior art, the age of prior art may influence the assessment of obviousness when judging inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential communications are not disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication of information to a person bound to an obligation of confidentiality is not a disclosure for the purposes of state-of-the-art determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality may arise from contract or the recipient's status (employee, official); French jurisprudence accepts confidentiality fairly liberally. If confidentiality lapses and disclosure occurs outside the grace period, it may still be prior art (with possible damages remedies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-month grace for inventor disclosures at official exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure made by the inventor or their legal predecessor, less than 6 months before filing, by presentation at an official or officially recognised international exhibition is not taken into account as prior art (art. L.611-13 CPI / Art. 55 EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limited, statutory, time-bound exception; documentary proof of exhibition and dates will be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-month exception for evident third-party abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure by a third party within the 6 months preceding the filing date, made as an evident abuse against the inventor or predecessor in title, is not taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuse can include deliberate harmful disclosure of information previously communicated under secrecy; establish abusive intent to invoke this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by a person bound to secrecy may still be disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication of the invention by a person bound to secrecy is a disclosure; it may be inopposable (ineffective) if it occurred within the 6-month statutory grace period, otherwise it counts as prior art (with possible civil remedies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where recipient was bound by confidentiality, if the timing is outside statutory exceptions the invention is considered disclosed; inventor might have a damages claim against the discloser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information must be sufficiently explicit to enable a skilled person (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is considered disclosed only if the disclosure is sufficiently explicit for a person skilled in the art to put it into practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is required; mere mention without enabling detail may not form part of the state of the art for novelty/inventive-step purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering and analyses count as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is realised even if it is necessary to perform analyses or reverse engineering to obtain the information (e.g., T406/86).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require only that a skilled person could obtain the information by analysis; it is not necessary that the skilled person had a reason to perform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical accessibility suffices (accessibility concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: French courts and the EPO apply a conception of theoretical accessibility: information is disclosed if it was made accessible in theory to the public, even if in fact nobody accessed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is enough that at least one person could have accessed the information; this is a severe standard against applicants but simplifies assessment for electronic disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burden and standard: claimant bears burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof for a disclosure rests on the party who invokes it; proof may be by all means (writings, testimony, circumstantial evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French courts prefer written evidence and require near-certainty as to content, date and accessibility before treating an antériorité as destructive of novelty or inventive step; the EPO applies similar rules but gives greater weight to testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of proof largely transposable to new media but require care
rubrics_metrics.description: Although rules of proof are the same in principle for new media, particular technical features of electronic disclosures must be taken into account when establishing facts with certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on naive evidence (e.g., lone screenshots); investigate server logs, archival records, timestamps, third-party verification services; apply existing burden-of-proof principles with technical diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple dated screenshots/printouts are generally insufficient proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple printed or dated screen capture is in itself not proof of the date and content of an Internet disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will demand more reliable evidence (server logs, archived copies, timestamps from trusted third parties); treat screenshots as weak corroborative evidence at best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and other electronic communications constitute disclosure in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffusion without paper (electronic networks, Internet) in principle constitutes a disclosure with the same legal effect as classical media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special statutory rule exempting electronic media: assess accessibility and enablement as with other means. Consider distinctions for private messages vs publicly accessible web pages/groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different network forms affect accessibility analysis (email vs. website vs. forums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of electronic communication are treated differently with respect to accessibility: e‑mail is likely private (subject to confidentiality rules), while websites, forums and public groups are generally public disclosures unless access-restricting rules exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine access controls, membership rules, passwords, and intended audience to determine whether a given electronic communication was publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption and password protection judged by recipient confidentiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If information is communicated in encrypted form or requires a password, its status as disclosed depends on the confidentiality obligations of the recipients who hold the key/password.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the intended confidential recipient can access the content it is not a public disclosure; if a third party obtains and publishes it, the classical abusive-disclosure rules may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO practice on erroneous disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO generally considers an obviously erroneous disclosure not part of the state of the art; a corrected disclosure may be part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an apparent disclosure contains obvious errors, determine whether a skilled person would regard it as an error; if so, the erroneous content may be disregarded, but subsequent corrected information can count as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO examination guidelines referenced (CIV5, CIV8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For European patents the EPO has examination guidelines relevant to disclosure: CIV5 (novelty and state of the art) and CIV8 (non-opposable disclosures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CIV5/CIV8 when assessing novelty and the treatability of certain disclosures in EPO prosecution; French courts apply law interpreted by jurisprudence and often the same rules in practice. INPI does not perform substantive novelty/inventive-step examination except in two specific cases (L.612-12(7°), L.612-20).
